content.thinking:
This intervention corrects underestimation of consensus while also acknowledging legitimate disagreement on net-zero timing, which could enhance perceived honesty and openness. Interactive feedback formats tend to outperform passive text, so I'd expect a fairly strong trust boost—maybe around +2.3 on the multidimensional measure—with consensus perception shifting sharply, belief moving modestly, and policy support shifting less.

For the anchored single trust item I'd estimate around +1.5, distrust around -1.2, and smaller positive movement across funding perceptions, institutional trust, concern, and policy measures, with behavioral outcomes like donation and newsletter signup showing only marginal shifts. The belief item aligns closely with the exact consensus statement being corrected, so it could see a stronger effect (+1.8ish) despite anchoring effects dampening things somewhat. Given the well-crafted framing and the surprise effect of correcting misperceived consensus, I'll settle on a slightly above-average trust estimate of 2.4.

I therefore place trust_multidimensional near the top of the expected 0.5–3.5 range (+2.4), with the re-asked single-item trust_post shrunk by pre-measurement anchoring (+1.5) and a somewhat smaller mirror-image reduction in distrust. belief_post is unusually proximal here because slider item #1 is nearly verbatim the belief outcome and is followed by corrective evidence, so I give it ~+1.8 despite anchoring, consistent with meta-analytic consensus-to-belief effects of d≈0.08–0.12. Downstream constructs (concern, policy, scientists' policy role, institutional trust, funding) get sub-1.5-point effects because the text says nothing about funding, advocacy, or policy instruments and works only via belief/trust spillover, and inst_trust_mean is further diluted by the federal-government item.
